prime.problem: Append-only storage makes writes fast and snapshots cheap, but an update or a delete is just one more record: old bytes stay on disk, and deleted data stays readable until every file, replica and backup is rewritten. And when one change must commit in two different systems, XA's two-phase commit can leave both holding locks while its coordinator is down.
prime.fits: Builds on the money-transfer card, which avoided distributed transactions with a log, and on the correlated-failure card's multiplied availabilities. This card shows the two costs that design sidesteps: compaction and deletion in immutable stores, and blocking in 2PC.
expect: compaction: newest record per key, then delete old files
tombstones must outlive every older copy
prime.goal: Explain why a delete in an append-only store is a write that must be compacted (and why erasure is harder still), and trace 2PC through a coordinator crash to show why prepared participants block and how much that costs.

attend: In the two-segment example, why can't compaction of seg2 alone drop u1's tombstone?
Why does a GDPR erasure request need more than a tombstone?

must: Append-only → an update or delete is a new record (a tombstone) → old records stay until compaction rewrites files keeping the newest per key → disk holds 3× the live data before compacting here, and compaction work must be tuned

A tombstone hides older copies → drop it while an older segment still holds the key and the old value reappears → it must outlive every older copy → and true deletion must reach every file, replica and backup

2PC: PREPARE → every participant durably promises (YES) and keeps its locks → the coordinator logs COMMIT → tells everyone → a YES voter can't decide alone, because only the coordinator's log knows the outcome

Coordinator crashes after the votes → every participant stays in doubt, holding locks for the whole outage (30 s = 3,750× the normal 8 ms hold) → and every participant plus the coordinator must be up: 0.999<sup>3</sup> → 129.5 min/month down vs 43.2 for one part
elevated: Messages grow as 4n but latency stays two round trips, because each phase goes to all participants in parallel → the cost of adding a participant is availability and failure amplification, not latency
reference: Datomic excision, CouchDB's append-only B-tree, RethinkDB's young blocks
the source's four XA complaints by name

retrieve.q: Explain why an append-only store gets high write throughput and cheap snapshots, and what it pays for them.
answer: writes only append, never seek and overwrite; old data is never changed, so a snapshot is just a position
the price: extra disk for dead records, and background compaction work to reclaim it
and deletion becomes a write whose effect is only complete after compaction everywhere

retrieve.q: Walk through 2PC for the order service (database + queue) with the coordinator crashing after logging COMMIT: message by message, and the state of each participant.
answer: PREPARE × 2 → each writes YES durably, keeps locks, replies YES × 2 (4 messages)
coordinator logs COMMIT (the commit point) and crashes
db and queue are prepared and in doubt, holding locks
on restart the coordinator reads its log and sends COMMIT; only then do they commit and release

retrieve.q: A team wants XA across the orders database, a payments database and a queue (n = 3). What do you tell them about availability, and what do you propose instead?
answer: 12 messages, and every part plus the coordinator must be up: 0.999<sup>4</sup> = 99.60%, about 172.5 min down a month vs 43.2
a coordinator crash blocks all three while holding locks
instead: commit once to one log and let each system consume it with request-id dedup; a slow consumer lags instead of blocking

compare.q: The LSM-tree card compacts sorted runs for read speed; this card compacts for space and deletion. What drives compaction in each view, and what goes wrong if it falls behind?
answer: LSM view: reads must check more runs until they merge, so read amplification grows
this card's view: dead records waste disk and deleted data stays readable
falling behind: slow reads and full disks; dropping tombstones too early: resurrected data

compare.q: 2PC blocks when its coordinator dies; Raft elects a new leader in under a second. Why can't 2PC's participants just elect a new coordinator, and how does Spanner combine the two?
answer: 2PC needs every participant to agree (atomic commit); consensus needs only a majority to agree on a value
the decision lives only in the coordinator's log, so a new coordinator can't know it
Spanner replicates each participant and the coordinator with Paxos, so the decision survives and a crashed coordinator is replaced instead of waited for

predict.q: Move the XA transaction's participants across a continent: the normal lock hold becomes one 69 ms round trip instead of 8 ms. At 1,000 transactions/s, how many transactions are in doubt when the coordinator crashes, and how many times the normal hold does a 30 s restart cost? Commit first.
predict.answer: In doubt at the crash = 1,000 × 0.069 = 69 transactions (vs 8). A 30 s outage is 30 / 0.069 ≈ 435× the normal hold (vs 3,750×). The ratio looks milder only because the normal hold itself is 8.6× longer; every transaction now holds its locks 69 ms even when nothing fails, and more of them are caught in doubt.

apply.task: Extend two_phase_commit in code/compaction-xa.py: make one participant vote NO and check that both end aborted with 8 messages for n = 2. Then add a recover(coordinator_log) step that, after crash_after_votes=True, reads the logged decision and finishes phase 2. Finally, add a timeout in prepare: a participant that hasn't voted yet may abort alone. Show it can't do the same once it has voted.
apply.done: The NO run prints ABORT with both participants aborted; the crash run leaves both prepared until recover commits them; and your timeout code aborts an unvoted participant but refuses to touch a prepared one, with a one-line comment saying why.
